dominantMode: Historical argument + source analysis + historiographical interpretation
cleanRule: Ancient History = construct an historical argument + analyse and interpret sources (archaeological and written) + evaluate differing historical interpretations + use historical concepts (causation, continuity and change, perspectives, significance, contestability)
leaderboardTip: HSC Ancient History rewards specific historical evidence — named sources (Papyrus Lansing, Karnak reliefs, Amarna Letters), named historians (Shaw, Tyldesley, Redford), and named archaeological sites. Generic statements about 'ancient Egyptians' without specific source reference cannot reach Band 5. Always link evidence to the historical argument.

ancientSocieties_OptionA.title: Option A: New Kingdom Egypt society to the death of Amenhotep III
ancientSocieties_OptionA.contentFocus: Through an investigation of key features of New Kingdom Egypt society to the death of Amenhotep III, and their interrelated nature, students examine a range of archaeological and written sources and relevant historiographical issues.

survey.title: Survey
dotPoints: Geographical setting, natural features and resources of New Kingdom Egypt and its neighbours
Significant sites: Thebes, Valley of the Kings, Malkata

socialStructureAndPoliticalOrganisation.title: Social Structure and Political Organisation
dotPoints: Roles and images of the pharaoh, the concept of maat
Roles of the vizier and members of the religious, administrative and military elites
Nature and role of the army
Roles and status of women: royal and non-royal
Scribes, artisans and agricultural workers

economy.title: The Economy
dotPoints: Importance of the Nile: agriculture, animal husbandry, transport
Economic exchange: barter and taxation
Impact of empire: booty, tribute and trade
Occupations, crafts and industry: wood, stone and metal
Technology: tools, building materials, techniques and construction

religionDeathAndBurial.title: Religion, Death and Burial
dotPoints: Gods, goddesses, cults and priesthoods including Amun-Re, Osiris
Festivals: Opet, Beautiful Feast of the Valley, Heb-Sed Festival
Myths and legends: Creation myth, Osiris myth
Funerary customs, rituals and texts: afterlife concepts, mummification
The Book of the Dead and the Amduat (Book of What is in the Netherworld)
Temples — architecture and function: Karnak, Luxor, Deir el-Bahri
Tombs — architecture and decoration: Thebes

culturalAndEverydayLife.title: Cultural and Everyday Life
dotPoints: Art: sculpture, jewellery and wall paintings
Writing and literature — love poetry, Papyrus Lansing: Be a Scribe, Wisdom Literature: the Instruction of Ani
Leisure activities
Health of New Kingdom Egyptians in this period as revealed by human remains

coreStudy.title: Core Study: Cities of Vesuvius — Pompeii and Herculaneum
coreStudy.contentFocus: Students investigate the range and nature of archaeological and written sources for the study of the cities of Pompeii and Herculaneum, and explore issues relating to reconstruction and conservation of the past.

dotPoints: The geographical setting and natural features of Campania
The eruption of AD 79 and its impact on Pompeii and Herculaneum
Early discoveries and the changing nature of excavations in the 19th and 20th centuries
Representations of Pompeii and Herculaneum over time

sourceAnalysis.description: Explaining the meaning and value of sources for historical inquiry; analysing sources for different perspectives; analysing and synthesising evidence from different source types; identifying problems relating to sources
keyQuestions: What type of source is it (archaeological, written, iconographic)?
Who created it, when, and for what purpose?
What does it reveal about the topic?
What are its limitations and biases?
How does it compare with other available sources?
What problems exist in using this source as historical evidence?

historiography.description: Analysing and evaluating differing interpretations and representations of the past made by historians and others
keyHistorians: Ian Shaw — Oxford History of Ancient Egypt
Joyce Tyldesley — specialist in Egyptian queens and personalities
Donald Redford — Akhenaten and New Kingdom Egypt
Alan Gardiner — Egyptian grammar and sources
Cyril Aldred — New Kingdom Egypt and Akhenaten

Band6.descriptor: Demonstrates extensive knowledge and understanding of a range of historical features, people, places, events and developments, and their significance. Demonstrates comprehensive understanding of continuity and change over time. Demonstrates comprehensive understanding of different perspectives of individuals and groups in the past. Analyses and interprets sources for evidence and synthesises evidence. Evaluates differing interpretations and representations of the past. Demonstrates sophisticated understanding and use of historical concepts and terms. Communicates a high level and sustained argument through well-structured and comprehensive texts.
keyFeatures: Extensive knowledge across historical features, people, places, events and developments
Comprehensive understanding of continuity and change
Analyses AND interprets sources for evidence — AND synthesises evidence across sources
Sophisticated understanding and use of historical concepts and terms
High level, SUSTAINED argument through well-structured and COMPREHENSIVE texts

Band5.descriptor: Demonstrates thorough knowledge and understanding of a range of historical features, people, places, events and developments, and their significance. Demonstrates a well-developed understanding of continuity and change over time. Demonstrates a well-developed understanding of different perspectives of individuals and groups in the past. Analyses and interprets sources for evidence. Analyses differing interpretations and representations of the past. Demonstrates thorough understanding and use of historical concepts and terms. Communicates a coherent and sustained argument through well-structured and comprehensive texts.
keyFeatures: Thorough knowledge of historical features, people, places, events and developments
Well-developed understanding of continuity and change
Analyses and interprets sources for evidence (synthesises at Band 6 — analyses at Band 5)
Thorough understanding and use of historical concepts and terms
Coherent and sustained argument through well-structured and comprehensive texts

Band4.descriptor: Demonstrates sound knowledge and understanding of a range of historical features, people, places, events and developments, and their significance. Demonstrates sound understanding of continuity and change over time. Demonstrates sound understanding of different perspectives of individuals and groups in the past. Uses sources for evidence. Discusses interpretations and representations of the past. Demonstrates understanding of historical concepts and terms. Communicates a general argument through well-structured texts.
keyFeatures: Sound knowledge of historical features, people, places, events and developments
Sound understanding of continuity and change
USES sources for evidence (analyses at Band 5)
Understanding of historical concepts and terms

Band3.descriptor: Demonstrates basic understanding of historical features, people, places, events, and their significance. Identifies features of continuity and change over time. Demonstrates basic understanding of different perspectives of individuals and groups in the past. Makes reference to sources. Identifies interpretations and representations of the past. Uses basic historical concepts and terms. Communicates basic information through descriptive texts.
keyFeatures: Makes reference to sources (uses at Band 4)

Band2.descriptor: Describes historical features, people, places and events. Recognises aspects of continuity and/or change. Demonstrates limited understanding of different perspectives of individuals and groups in the past. Makes reference to sources. Uses limited historical concepts and terms. Provides limited information in narrative style.

Band1.descriptor: Performance reported as Band 1 indicates that the minimum standard expected was not demonstrated.

dominant_question_types: Assess/evaluate the significance of a feature of New Kingdom Egypt society (e.g. role of the pharaoh, importance of the Nile)
Analyse the nature and role of a specific aspect of society (e.g. women, the army, religion)
To what extent does evidence suggest... (continuity and change, significance)
Evaluate the usefulness and/or limitations of a source or type of source for the study of New Kingdom Egypt
Assess differing historical interpretations of a feature of New Kingdom Egypt society
How adequately do the sources reveal... (everyday life, religion, social structure)
ancient_history_specific_tips: ALWAYS name specific sources — archaeological (Karnak reliefs, Deir el-Bahri mortuary temple, Malkata palace), written (Papyrus Lansing, Instruction of Ani, Annals of Thutmose III) and iconographic (wall paintings, sculpture). Generic references to 'sources' or 'evidence' earn Band 3 at best.
ALWAYS evaluate sources — comment on their value (what they reveal) AND their limitations (bias, purpose, incompleteness). For Band 5-6, analysis of source reliability is essential.

Include historiography — name historians (Shaw, Tyldesley, Redford, Aldred, Bryan) and their interpretations, especially where they differ. Evaluating competing interpretations distinguishes Band 5 from Band 6.
Use historical concepts explicitly — label your arguments using causation, continuity and change, perspectives, significance and contestability. Don't just describe events.
Link evidence to argument — every named source should support a specific historical claim. Do not list sources without connecting them to the argument.
For continuity and change questions: identify what stayed the same as well as what changed, and assess the pace and extent of change.
common_errors: Describing historical events without constructing an argument ('The pharaoh was important because...' without evaluating significance or causation).
Naming sources without evaluating them — 'wall paintings show...' without commenting on value or limitation.
Ignoring historiography — not naming any modern historians or their interpretations.
Describing both sides of a debate without making a judgement — Band 5-6 requires evaluation, not just discussion.
Confusing continuity and change — not distinguishing what persisted from what transformed.
Using general terms ('ancient Egyptians', 'the sources') without specific names.

argument_construction_steps: State a clear historical thesis or argument in response to the question.
Identify the historical period, context, and relevant aspects of New Kingdom Egypt.
Present evidence from named archaeological and/or written sources to support the argument.
Evaluate the sources — what do they reveal, and what are their limitations?
Integrate at least one historical interpretation (named historian) and assess it.
Apply historical concepts: causation, continuity and change, significance, perspectives, contestability.
Conclude with a judgement that directly answers the question.
source_analysis_steps: Identify the source type (archaeological, written, iconographic).
State what the source reveals about the topic (its historical value).
Identify the source's perspective, purpose, and likely audience.
Comment on what the source does NOT reveal or may misrepresent (limitations).
Cross-reference with other source types where possible.
Link the source analysis to the historical argument.

before_output: Is a clear historical argument stated and sustained?
Are specific named sources cited (archaeological, written, iconographic)?
Is historiography included (named historian and their view)?
Are historical concepts used explicitly (causation, significance, continuity/change)?
Does the response address perspectives (individual, group, gender, class)?
Is the response specific to New Kingdom Egypt to the death of Amenhotep III?
Does the conclusion directly address the question with a judgement?
band6_checklist: Extensive, specific historical knowledge across multiple aspects of the topic.
Comprehensive understanding of continuity and change — both identified and assessed.
Sources analysed, interpreted AND synthesised across source types.
Differing historical interpretations EVALUATED — not just described.
Sophisticated use of historical concepts and terminology throughout.
High-level sustained argument — not a narrative or list of facts.
Comprehensive texts — detailed, well-structured, covering the breadth of the question.

target_band_selection_rule.Band6: Extensive knowledge, comprehensive continuity/change analysis, synthesis of multiple source types, evaluation of differing historiographical interpretations, sophisticated historical concepts, sustained high-level argument.
target_band_selection_rule.Band5: Thorough knowledge, well-developed continuity/change, analysis and interpretation of sources, analysis of interpretations (not full evaluation), thorough historical concepts, coherent sustained argument.
target_band_selection_rule.Band4: Sound knowledge, sound continuity/change, uses sources for evidence (references without deep analysis), discusses interpretations, understands historical concepts, general argument.
target_band_selection_rule.Band3: Basic knowledge, identifies continuity/change, makes reference to sources, identifies interpretations, basic terms, descriptive text.
target_band_selection_rule.Band2: Describes events, recognises change, limited terms, narrative style.
target_band_selection_rule.Band1: Do not generate unless explicitly requested.

forbidden_behaviours: Do not construct a response that only narrates events without building an historical argument.
Do not use generic source references — always name specific sources.
Do not ignore historiography — always include at least one named historian.
Do not describe interpretations without evaluating them at Band 5-6.
Do not confuse the topic period — all evidence must be specific to New Kingdom Egypt to the death of Amenhotep III.

ancientHistoryNote: Ancient History CUBE marking has important differences from Science and HSIE subjects. The Underline step should identify: named historical figures, named sites (Karnak, Malkata, Thebes), named source types (wall paintings, papyri, reliefs), named historical concepts (maat, continuity, significance), and any directive verbs that trigger source evaluation or historiographical judgement. Planning arrows should show: thesis → evidence (named sources) → source analysis (value/limitation) → historiography (named historian) → judgement.
